\chapter{Where It Hurts --- Eye, Mouth, Throat, Pain, Fever}
\label{ch:donde-duele}
\hlchaptermodality{286}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the eye, the mouth and the throat in Spanish, and say that there is a pain or a fever.}

Complete ES-C286-fiebre: name all five, and separate the three places from the two things that are wrong.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el ojo]{el ojo — the same eye as English, from far enough back}

\label{lesson:ES-C286-ojo}



\begin{quote}
Before a new run: what does \emph{precocious} literally mean? (Cooked early.) And who is the \emph{enfermera} named after? (The patient.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la cabeza — where this one is.
  \item la mano — the other body word you have.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{O-jo}, stress on the first syllable. The \emph{j} is a hard rasp at the back of the mouth, the \emph{jota}, with no English equivalent. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el ojo} — \textquotedblleft{}the eye.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{oculus}, and the road from \emph{oculus} to \emph{ojo} runs through a change Spanish made and its neighbours made differently: the \emph{cl} left in \emph{oc'lu}, once the unstressed vowel dropped, hardened into the \emph{jota} you are now saying — a sound Latin never had at all.

English has the loans, and they are unmistakable: \textbf{ocular}, \textbf{binocular}, a \textbf{monocle}, and to \textbf{inoculate}, which was a gardener's word first, for setting an eye — a bud — into another plant.

And English \textbf{eye} is the cousin, not a borrowing. \emph{Oculus} and \emph{eye} come down from one ancient root by two different roads, one through Latin and one through Germanic, which is why they share almost no letters and mean precisely the same thing.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The \emph{jota} is a Spanish invention.

It is not in Latin, and it is not in Italian or French, which had the same material to work with. When a word has one, you are hearing something that happened in Spain and nowhere else.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el ojo}, then \emph{los ojos}
  \item \emph{oculus} and \emph{ojo}, slowly, and hear the \emph{cl} harden
  \item \emph{la cabeza} and \emph{el ojo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the Latin behind \emph{ojo}? (\emph{Oculus}.) Is English \emph{eye} borrowed from it? (No — it is the cousin, down the Germanic road.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la boca]{la boca — the cheek that took the mouth's job}

\label{lesson:ES-C286-boca}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: is English \emph{eye} borrowed from \emph{oculus}? (No — it is the cousin.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el ojo — the last one, and its neighbour on the face.
  \item la cabeza — which Spanish did not replace, unlike this one.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{BO-ca}, stress on the first syllable. The \emph{c} before \emph{a} is a hard \emph{k}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la boca} — \textquotedblleft{}the mouth.\textquotedblright{}

Latin had \textbf{os}, \textbf{oris} for the mouth, and that is the word English borrowed for \textbf{oral} and \textbf{orifice}. Spanish does not use it. Spanish uses \textbf{bucca}, which in Latin meant the cheek — specifically a cheek puffed out, the one a trumpeter uses.

So the lively word from the street pushed the official one out of the job. That is a swap Spanish declined to make for the head, where \emph{cabeza} is still \emph{caput} plain and simple, and made without hesitation for the mouth. Which words get replaced is not predictable; it only ever looks obvious afterwards.

English kept both ends of the Latin. \textbf{Buccal} is the medical adjective for the cheek. To \textbf{debouch} is to come out of a mouth — said of rivers, and of armies leaving a narrow pass.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two body words, and two completely different histories.

\emph{Ojo} is the inherited word doing the job it always did. \emph{Boca} is an upstart that took the job from another word. Both are ordinary, and only one of them is quiet about where it came from.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la boca}
  \item \emph{el ojo} and \emph{la boca}
  \item \emph{oris} and \emph{bucca}, the word that lost and the word that won
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{bucca} mean in Latin? (The cheek.) Which Latin word did it push out? (\emph{Os}, \emph{oris} — which English kept in \emph{oral}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la garganta]{la garganta — a word made out of a noise}

\label{lesson:ES-C286-garganta}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{bucca} mean in Latin? (The cheek.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la boca — the opening this one sits behind.
  \item el agua — what goes down it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{gar-GAN-ta}, stress in the middle. Both \emph{g} sounds are hard, and both \emph{r} sounds are single taps. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la garganta} — \textquotedblleft{}the throat.\textquotedblright{}

This one is not inherited from a tidy Latin word so much as assembled out of a noise. Latin had \textbf{gurgulio} for the windpipe and \textbf{gargarizare} for gargling, and both are the sound itself, said twice: \emph{gar-gar}.

English does the same imitation over and over. To \textbf{gargle}. To \textbf{gurgle}. To \textbf{regurgitate}. A \textbf{gorge}, which is a throat first and a narrow valley second, because a valley of that shape looks like one.

Words like this are worth noticing because they escape the usual account. Almost all of your vocabulary is either inherited or borrowed. A few words are simply what the thing sounds like — and those can turn up in unrelated languages with no contact between them whatsoever.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three places on the body, and now you can say where.

\emph{El ojo}, \emph{la boca}, \emph{la garganta}. What is still missing is the other half of the sentence: what is actually wrong. That is the next two.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la garganta}
  \item \emph{gar-gar}, then \emph{garganta}, and hear where the word came from
  \item \emph{el ojo}, \emph{la boca}, \emph{la garganta}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \emph{garganta} come from? (The noise of gargling.) Which English words are the same imitation? (\emph{Gargle}, \emph{gurgle}, \emph{gorge}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el dolor]{el dolor — and the word that stopped hurting}

\label{lesson:ES-C286-dolor}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: where does \emph{garganta} come from? (The noise of gargling.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la garganta — one of the places this can be.
  \item ¿cómo está usted? — the question this answers.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{do-LOR}, stress on the second syllable, as the lack of a written accent tells you for a word ending in \emph{r}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el dolor} — \textquotedblleft{}the pain.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{dolor}, arriving with almost nothing worn off it, from \textbf{dolere}, to hurt. This is the word that turns a body part into a complaint: a pain of the head, a pain of the throat.

English has it in the mournful register only: \textbf{doleful}, \textbf{dolorous}, and \textbf{condolence} — to hurt together with somebody.

And \textbf{indolent}, which is the surprise of the family. \emph{In-dolens} is feeling no pain, and it began as a medical word: an indolent sore is one that does not hurt. From there it slid to feeling no effort, and finally to lazy. The pain fell out of the word altogether.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now answer with more than \emph{bien} or \emph{regular}.

A place and a trouble is a whole sentence in any language. You have three places and, from here, two troubles.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el dolor}
  \item \emph{dolor de cabeza}
  \item \emph{dolor de garganta}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{dolere} mean? (To hurt.) What did \emph{indolent} mean first? (Feeling no pain.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la fiebre]{la fiebre — one Latin word, borrowed twice, centuries apart}

\label{lesson:ES-C286-fiebre}



\begin{quote}
Before the last of the five: what does \emph{dolere} mean? (To hurt.) And where does \emph{garganta} come from? (The noise of gargling.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el dolor — the other thing that can be wrong.
  \item cierto — where you last watched a stressed \emph{e} open into \emph{ie}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{FIE-bre}, stress on the first syllable. The \emph{ie} is one glide, and the \emph{b} between vowels is soft. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la fiebre} — \textquotedblleft{}the fever.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{febris}, with the stressed \emph{e} opening into \emph{ie} once again — \emph{febris} to \emph{fiebre}, the change you have now watched in \emph{cierto} and in \emph{puerta}, and can predict without being told.

English \textbf{fever} is that same \emph{febris}, borrowed into Old English long before the Normans arrived, at a time when a Latin medical word was worth having and an English one did not exist. Then the doctors borrowed it a second time, unworn, as \textbf{febrile}.

Two borrowings of one word, a thousand years apart: the early one goes to the sickroom and the late one to the textbook. That split is so regular in English that you can often date a word by how ordinary it sounds.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \emph{el ojo}, \emph{la boca}, \emph{la garganta}, \emph{el dolor}, \emph{la fiebre}.

Three of them are places and two are troubles, and the two halves fit together. \emph{Dolor de garganta}, \emph{dolor de cabeza} — a place and a trouble joined by a word you have had since the beginning. That is a real sentence, built entirely out of five new words and one small old one.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la fiebre}
  \item \emph{tengo fiebre}
  \item all five in order — \emph{el ojo}, \emph{la boca}, \emph{la garganta}, \emph{el dolor}, \emph{la fiebre}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which vowel change turned \emph{febris} into \emph{fiebre}? (Stressed \emph{e} into \emph{ie}.) How many times did English borrow this word? (Twice — \emph{fever}, then \emph{febrile}.) And what did \emph{indolent} mean first? (Feeling no pain.)
\end{tcolorbox}
